rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story a reporter might write and a story REI should actively pitch. Its refusal of "Record dividend lands amid union drives — what REI owes its workers vs its members" is the adult move; B's "Trade-in counters and repair benches arrive at REI stores as workers organize" is real newsroom bait, but it invites a labor frame the company may not be ready to own. B has sharper raw variety, especially "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear," but that headline overstates the supplied fact: not disclosed is not the same as refused.
gaps_in_A: Misses a strong standalone accountability/data angle around "the share of sales from used gear not disclosed"; it folds that hole into proof needs instead of recognizing it could be the story.
The customer-service angle, "What an REI membership now gets you," is useful but thinner than the operations and co-op angles unless REI provides real valuation, pricing, and turnaround examples.
"a repair counter in every store" may be too concrete for the facts supplied; the update says members can get repairs at any store, not that every store has a full repair counter.
gaps_in_B: "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear" overclaims. The facts say the share is not disclosed; they do not say REI refused to answer.

"pushing customers to buy used" is loaded and not fully grounded. The update says trade-in, resale, and repair support sustainability commitments; it does not say REI is pushing used purchases over new gear.

"Trade-in counters and repair benches arrive" invents store-level mechanics. The set later asks whether these are full-service benches or intake counters, which proves the headline got ahead of the facts.
It treats the union angle as one of "four viable shapes" instead of mostly a risk to prepare for. That may land press, yes, but possibly the kind that makes the client wonder why they hired you.
